summary: Describes the BLAKE2 cryptographic hash function and provides the specification and C source code. BLAKE2b suits 64-bit platforms and BLAKE2s smaller ones. It can be keyed directly, so it also works as a MAC.

eli5.summary: BLAKE2 turns any data into a short fingerprint, and can mix in a secret key to make the fingerprint prove who made it.

subtitle: A fast hash function with a built-in key, published with its full specification and reference C code.

tldr.problem: Applications needed an efficient hash function and keyed authentication code, and the BLAKE2 specification and code were not conveniently available to the Internet community.
tldr.mechanism: BLAKE2b (64-bit platforms) and BLAKE2s (8- to 32-bit platforms) split the padded key and data into blocks, run each through a compression function built from a mixing function G, and return the first nn bytes of the final state.
tldr.outcome: The RFC gives the algorithm, standard digest sizes with OIDs, worked traces and C source. It makes no independent security claim and is not an Internet Standard.

today: RFC 7693 is an Informational document from the Independent Submission stream. It is not an Internet Standards Track specification, and it has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 7693 describes the BLAKE2 cryptographic hash function, designed by Jean-Philippe Aumasson, Samuel Neves, Zooko Wilcox-O'Hearn and Christian Winnerlein. It makes the algorithm specification and C source code available to the Internet community.

There are two flavors. BLAKE2b is optimized for 64-bit platforms and produces digests of 1 to 64 bytes. BLAKE2s is optimized for 8- to 32-bit platforms and produces digests of 1 to 32 bytes.

BLAKE2 has a built-in keying mechanism, so it does not need a separate HMAC construction to act as a message authentication code. The RFC presents it as a more efficient alternative to the US Secure Hash Algorithms and HMAC-SHA (RFC 6234), and calls BLAKE2s-128 a fast drop-in replacement for MD5 and HMAC-MD5 in legacy applications (RFC 6151).
sections.eli5: BLAKE2 is a recipe for making a short fingerprint of any data. One version is tuned for big modern computers and the other for small ones.

sections.title: Parameters, Constants and Conventions
sections.content:
The two variants differ in word size, number of rounds, block size and rotation constants. All arithmetic is on 64-bit words in BLAKE2b and 32-bit words in BLAKE2s, and byte streams are read as words in little-endian order, least-significant byte first.

The parameter block is word p[0] = 0x0101kknn, with all other words zero. Here nn is the hash size in bytes and kk is the key size in bytes, with kk = 00 for unkeyed hashing. The initial state comes from the Initialization Vector IV, defined from the fractional parts of the square roots of the first eight primes. The RFC notes that the BLAKE2b IV equals the SHA-512 IV and the BLAKE2s IV equals the SHA-256 IV.

The message word order in each round comes from a table called SIGMA. For BLAKE2b, which has two extra rounds, SIGMA[10..11] = SIGMA[0..1]. The RFC also notes that the original BLAKE2 paper defines salting, personalization and tree hashing through parameter block fields this document does not define.
sections.eli5: Each version has its own settings, like different sized boxes and a different number of shuffles. Both start from fixed starting numbers so everyone begins the same way.

sections.title: The Mixing and Compression Functions
sections.content:
The core is the mixing function G. It takes four entries of a 16-word working vector v plus two message words x and y, and updates them using additions modulo 2**w, XORs and rotations by the constants R1 to R4.

The compression function F takes the state h, a message block m, a 2w-bit offset counter t and a final-block flag f. It copies the state into the first half of v and the IV into the second half, XORs the counter into v[12] and v[13], and inverts all bits of v[14] if this is the last block. It then runs 12 rounds for BLAKE2b or 10 for BLAKE2s. Each round applies G eight times, four on columns and four on diagonals, using message words picked by SIGMA. The new state is h[i] ^ v[i] ^ v[i + 8] for each of the eight words.
sections.eli5: G is a blender that stirs a few numbers together. F pours a block of your data into the blender over and over, then combines the result with what it already had.

sections.title: Padding and Computing a Digest
sections.content:
The key and data are split into dd blocks of bb bytes each. If a key is used (kk > 0), it is padded with zero bytes and becomes the first block. The last data block is padded with zeros to a full block. For an unkeyed empty message there is still one block, all zeros.

The state starts as the IV, with the parameter block XORed into h[0]. Every block except the last goes through F with a counter that grows by bb bytes each time and the final flag false. The last block goes through F with the final flag true, and the counter is the message length, plus bb if a key was used. The digest is the first nn bytes of the final state, read as little-endian words.

Appendix A traces BLAKE2b-512 over the three ASCII bytes abc, and Appendix B traces BLAKE2s-256 over the same input. The RFC says it does not include a full set of test vectors for lack of space.
sections.eli5: Your data is cut into equal boxes, and the last box is topped up with zeros. Each box is stirred in one after another, and the last stir gets a special mark. A secret key, if you have one, goes in as the very first box.

sections.title: Standard Digest Sizes and OIDs
sections.content:
An implementation MAY support a set of standard digest sizes for interoperability, for example in digital signatures, as long as the chosen parameters give enough security. The sizes are meant as drop-in replacements for MD5 and the matching SHA algorithms. Developers adapting BLAKE2 to ASN.1-based message formats SHOULD use the OID tree 1.3.6.1.4.1.1722.12.2. The same OID serves keyed and unkeyed hashing, since unkeyed hashing is just a zero-length key.

The RFC lists identifiers such as id-blake2b512 and id-blake2s256, with the target architecture, the collision security level and the OID suffix of each.
sections.eli5: The RFC gives each popular output size its own official name tag, so different programs can agree on exactly which version they mean.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document aims only to give convenient open-source access to BLAKE2. It says it wishes to make no independent assertion about the algorithm's security, and refers readers to the BLAKE book and the BLAKE2 paper for the cryptanalytic rationale.

The reference implementations in Appendices C and D may not erase sensitive data, such as secret keys, from process memory right after use. The RFC says this was left out to avoid bloat and that cleanup can be added if needed.
sections.eli5: The authors only share the recipe and do not promise it is unbreakable. Their sample code also does not wipe your secret key from memory, so add that yourself if you need it.
